messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 43
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ana had always taken pride in her work as a chef, the precision and creativity required to craft exquisite dishes for her restaurant's patrons. But it was during one particularly grueling dinner service that she began to feel an unshakeable fatigue, a creeping numbness that seeped into every aspect of her life. At first, she wrote it off as exhaustion, but weeks turned into months, and the symptoms persisted. A visit to her doctor revealed a shocking diagnosis: stage III cancer. The treatment was brutal – rounds of chemotherapy that left her body weakened and her senses reeling. There were moments during those dark days when Ana felt like she was living outside her own skin, watching herself go through the motions as if in a dream. The pain was constant, the nausea debilitating, and the fear suffocating. It's been two years since Ana completed treatment, but the memories of that time remain etched in her mind with an unsettling vividness. She recalls the hospital smells, the antiseptic tang that still makes her stomach turn. The sound of beeping machines, the feel of cold needles piercing her skin – it all comes flooding back with a sensory intensity that leaves her breathless. Ana has come to believe that her body is no longer trustworthy, that it's a fragile vessel prone to betrayal. Her physical reactions are now on high alert, ready to trigger at a moment's notice. She'll be in the kitchen, chopping vegetables or seasoning a dish, when suddenly she's back in that hospital room, feeling the weight of her mortality bearing down upon her. As a result, Ana has developed an arsenal of coping strategies designed to keep those memories at bay. She numbs herself with work, pushing through exhaustion to avoid any moments of quiet contemplation. She shies away from social events or activities that might bring her joy – what's the point when it can all be taken away in an instant? And she delays sleep, staying up late into the night, too anxious to let her guard down. The cost of these strategies has been high. Ana's relationship with her partner has grown strained, as if they're living separate lives under the same roof. Her work suffers, too – she's constantly on edge, unable to relax even when the kitchen is quiet and still. The smallest trigger can send her spiraling: a certain smell, a particular song, or a fleeting glance at her own reflection in a window. Ana's greatest fear is that this is all there is now – that she'll never be able to shake off the residue of illness, that her body will forever be on high alert. She grieves for the carefree person she once was, the one who laughed easily and loved with abandon. That person feels lost to her now, a distant memory from another lifetime. As Ana navigates this fragile existence, she's begun to realize that she needs help. The emotional numbness, while protective in its own way, has become suffocating. She yearns for the capacity to feel again, to love without reservation, and to trust her body once more. It's a daunting prospect – confronting the memories she's worked so hard to suppress – but Ana knows it's the only way forward.
